q: Organisms that are restricted to a narrow range of salinity are termed:
Steno- means narrow and -haline refers to salinity, so stenohaline organisms tolerate only a narrow range of salinity. Euryhaline organisms tolerate a wide range.
Dependence of plants on light for their flowering is known as:

Zooplankton tide over unfavourable conditions by entering a stage of suspended development called:
Diapause is the stage of suspended development entered by zooplankton during unfavourable conditions. Hibernation is winter sleep and aestivation is summer sleep in…
Shorter limbs and ears in animals of colder regions, which minimise heat loss, illustrate:
Allen’s rule states that animals of colder regions have shorter limbs and ears to minimise heat loss. Thick fur and, in seals, a layer of blubber below the skin serve…

A triangular age pyramid with a broad pre-reproductive base indicates an expanding (growing) population. A bell shape indicates a stable population and an urn shape a…
A group of similar individuals living in a geographical area, sharing similar resources and capable of interbreeding is called a:
This is the definition of a population. A community consists of populations of different species living together, while a biome is a large climatic zone such as…

The carrying capacity of the habitat
The rate of emigration from the habitat
The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The population density at time zero

Which pair of factors ADDS individuals to a population?
In N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) – (D + E)], natality (B) and immigration (I) carry the plus sign, while mortality (D) and emigration (E) carry the minus sign.
In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN(K – N)/K, the population growth rate becomes zero when:
When N equals the carrying capacity K, the term (K – N)/K becomes zero, so dN/dt = 0 and the curve levels off as an asymptote. At N = K/2 the absolute growth rate is…
Thorns and secondary metabolites produced by plants are best described as:
Since herbivores are the predators of plants, plants produce thorns (morphological defence) and secondary metabolites or poisonous chemicals (chemical defence) to…
Cuscuta growing on a hedge plant is an example of:
Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that grows on hedge plants; it has lost its chlorophyll and leaves during evolution and derives nutrition from the host. It is classed…
The association between the sea anemone with stinging tentacles and the clown fish is an example of:
The clown fish gains protection from predators that avoid the stinging tentacles, but the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit from hosting the fish. Hence…
Mycorrhiza is a mutualistic association between:
Fungi and the roots of higher plants
In mycorrhizae, fungi associate with the roots of higher plants; the fungi help the plant absorb essential nutrients from the soil while the plant supplies the fungi…
Brood parasitism, also called nest or social parasitism, is best illustrated by:
A barnacle growing on the back of a whale
The Koel laying its eggs in the nest of a crow
A tick feeding on the skin of a dog
The cattle egret foraging beside grazing cattle
In brood parasitism the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of an unassuming host bird which rears them; the Koel and crow is the standard example. The barnacle…
Organisms develop adaptations primarily in order to:
Survive and reproduce better in their habitat
Adaptations are characteristics that help organisms survive and reproduce better in the habitat they live in.
Regions with hot climate and heavy rainfall give rise to which biome?
On a plot of mean annual temperature against mean annual precipitation, hot regions with heavy rainfall give rise to tropical forest, whereas hot regions with very…
Organisms that can tolerate a wide range of temperature are termed:
'Eury-' means wide and '-thermal' relates to temperature, so eurythermal organisms can tolerate a wide range of temperature.
On land, the factor that usually limits the distribution of organisms is:
On land, the quantity of water (rainfall) is usually the limiting factor for organisms, unlike in the oceans where quantity is not limiting but quality (salinity) is.
Salinity of ocean water is expressed in units of:
The salt concentration of water is measured as salinity, expressed in parts per thousand (ppt).
In aquatic habitats, the type of benthic (bottom-dwelling) life supported is decided mainly by:
The sediment characteristic of the bed
The number of fish species present
The temperature of the air above the water
In aquatic habitats the corresponding factor to soil is the sediment characteristic of the bed, which decides the type of benthic (bottom-dwelling) life.
Photosynthesis in deeper layers of oceans and lakes is limited chiefly because:
There are no plants in deep water
Deep water is too cold for any reaction
Fish consume all the available light
The availability of light on land is comparatively higher than in water, because water absorbs and scatters light; this limits photosynthesis in deeper layers of…
A marine invertebrate can survive only when the salinity of water is between 33 and 37 ppt. This organism is best described as:
Since the organism can tolerate only a narrow (33-37 ppt) range of salinity, it is stenohaline.
Which pair correctly represents the memory hook for temperature-tolerance terms?
The memory hook is: steno = narrow, eury = wide, thermal = temperature (and haline = salinity).
The dependence of flowering in many plants on the relative lengths of day and night is called:
Many plants depend on the duration of light for their flowering; this response is called photoperiodism.
Population density need not always be counted as absolute numbers of individuals because, depending on the species, it may instead be expressed as:
Population density need not always be counted as numbers; depending on the species it may be expressed as biomass (as for a huge banyan tree) or per cent cover (as…
The maintenance of a constant internal environment by an organism is called:
All organisms try to maintain a constant internal environment in order to sustain maximum functionality; this maintenance is called homeostasis.
Mammals maintain a body temperature of about 37°C regardless of the outside temperature. In summer, this is achieved partly by:
Sweating, whose evaporation cools the body
Reducing blood flow to the skin completely
In summer we sweat -- evaporation of sweat cools the body; in winter we shiver -- rapid muscle contraction produces heat.
Regulation gives an organism the greatest independence from the environment, but it comes at the cost of being:
Regulation gives the greatest independence from the environment, but it is energetically the most expensive strategy.
An organism whose body temperature changes in accordance with the outside temperature is called a:
Conformers are organisms whose body temperature (and osmotic concentration) changes in accordance with the outside temperature.
Migration as a response to stress is best described as:
Migration allows the organism to move away temporarily from the stressful habitat to a more hospitable area and return once the stressful period is over; this is…
Spores are formed by bacteria and lower plants chiefly in order to:
Spores are formed in bacteria and lower plants to tide over unfavourable conditions, ceasing metabolic activity until conditions improve.
Winter sleep seen in some animals, during which metabolic activity is greatly reduced, is called:
Hibernation is winter sleep in animals, during which metabolic activity is greatly reduced to conserve energy during cold periods.
Adaptations that relate to what an animal does, such as a lizard basking in the sun, are classified as:
Adaptations may be physiological (internal functioning), behavioural (what the animal does) or morphological (body form and structure); basking is a behaviour.
The sunken arrangement of stomata in deep pits, seen in desert plants, chiefly helps to:
Stomata are arranged in deep pits (sunken stomata) in desert plants to reduce water loss.
In desert plants such as Opuntia, leaves are reduced to spines while photosynthesis is carried out by:
Leaves are reduced to spines and photosynthesis is carried out by the flattened green stems, as in Opuntia.
Allen's rule explains why mammals of colder regions have shorter limbs and ears, because a smaller surface area relative to volume means:
A smaller surface area relative to volume means less heat is radiated away, which helps colder-region mammals minimise heat loss.
The thick fur covering colder-region animals reduces heat loss mainly by:
Trapping air, which is a poor conductor of heat
The body is covered by a thick fur which traps air and reduces heat loss.
Symptoms such as nausea, fatigue and heart palpitation experienced by a newcomer at high altitude are together called:
A newcomer at high altitude suffers from altitude sickness, with symptoms such as nausea, fatigue and heart palpitation.
The kangaroo rat of North American deserts meets almost its entire water requirement through:
Drinking large amounts of water daily
The kangaroo rat meets its entire water requirement through internal oxidation of fat (metabolic water) and concentrates its urine to lose very little water in excretion.
Diapause, seen in zooplankton of lakes and ponds, is best classified under which stress-response strategy?
Diapause is a stage of suspended development entered by zooplankton during unfavourable conditions, and is therefore an example of the 'Suspend' strategy.
Seeds of many plants reduce their metabolic activity and enter dormancy, germinating only when:
They are exposed to darkness permanently
They are placed in salt water
Seeds and other vegetative parts of plants reduce metabolic activity and enter dormancy, germinating only when conditions become favourable.
A thick cuticle on the leaf surface of desert plants primarily checks:
A thick cuticle on the leaf surface checks transpiration, helping desert plants conserve water.
At high altitude, the body decreases the binding capacity of haemoglobin chiefly so that:
Oxygen is released more readily to the tissues
Red blood cells are destroyed faster
Decreasing the binding capacity of haemoglobin means oxygen is released more readily to the tissues, helping compensate for the lower oxygen availability at high…
Evolutionary changes through natural selection take place at which level, linking ecology to evolution?
Since evolutionary changes through natural selection take place at the population level, population ecology is an important area of ecology that links ecology to…
All the teak trees of a forest patch would be considered an example of a:
A population is a group of similar individuals living in a geographical area, sharing similar resources, and capable of interbreeding -- for example all the teak…
The age distribution plot for a population, drawn with pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive bands, is called the:
The age distribution plot for a given population is called the age pyramid, typically drawn with three bands -- pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive.
A declining population is represented by an age pyramid of which shape?
A declining population gives an urn-shaped age pyramid, where the pre-reproductive base is narrower than the reproductive middle.
For a huge banyan tree, population density is more meaningfully expressed as:
The number of birds nesting in it
Population density need not always be counted as numbers; for a huge banyan tree it may be expressed as biomass rather than as a simple count of individuals.
For grass or lichens covering the ground, population density is best expressed as:
Population density may be expressed as per cent cover for species such as grass or lichens, where counting individuals is impractical.
For estimating the density of tigers in a forest, ecologists often count:
The number of leaves eaten daily
For a huge population like tigers, relative density is measured, such as the number of pug marks or faecal pellets counted, instead of the time-consuming absolute count.
All the lotus plants in a single pond would together form:
A community only, not a population
All the lotus plants in a pond, being similar individuals sharing resources and able to interbreed, form a population.
Birth rate is also referred to as:
Birth rate is also called natality -- the number of live births per one thousand individuals per year.
All the rats living in an abandoned dwelling, capable of interbreeding, together constitute:
All the rats in an abandoned dwelling, being similar individuals capable of interbreeding in a shared geographical area, together constitute a population.
If, over a given period, (B + I) is less than (D + E), the population will:
If (B + I) < (D + E), the population declines because more individuals are lost than added.
A population of 500 records, in one year, 80 births, 30 deaths, 15 immigrants and 25 emigrants. Its density at the end of that year is:
A population of 2,000 records 150 births, 200 deaths, 50 immigrants and 20 emigrants in a year. Its density at the end of that year is:
Exponential growth of a population occurs mainly when:
Resources such as food and space are unlimited
The population size is very small
Exponential growth occurs when resources (food and space) are unlimited, so every individual can realise its full reproductive potential.
In dN/dt = (b - d) × N, the term (b - d) is substituted with the symbol:
Substituting (b - d) = r gives the standard form dN/dt = rN, where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase.
The exponential growth curve, when population size is plotted against time, is described as:
Plotted against time, exponential growth gives an unbounded J-shaped curve.
When N is much smaller than K, the term (K - N)/K in the logistic equation is close to:
When N is small compared to K, (K-N)/K is close to 1, and growth is nearly exponential.
The logistic growth model is considered more realistic than the exponential model chiefly because:
No habitat has truly unlimited resources
It does not require the value of r
Because no habitat has truly unlimited resources, the logistic model is considered the more realistic of the two growth models.
Species that breed only once in their lifetime, investing all reproductive effort in a single event, include:
Pacific salmon fish and bamboo breed only once in a lifetime; most birds and mammals, in contrast, breed many times.
Oysters and pelagic fishes typically produce:
A small number of large-sized offspring
A large number of small-sized offspring
Oysters and pelagic fishes produce a large number of small-sized offspring, with little parental care and heavy losses, as part of their life-history strategy.
Populations tend to increase their reproductive fitness, a concept referred to in ecology as:
Populations tend to increase their reproductive fitness so as to survive better -- this is called Darwinian fitness, reflected in a high r value.
The specific life-history strategy a species evolves (breeding once vs many times, few large vs many small offspring) depends chiefly on:
The habitat and abiotic conditions it faces
Random chance with no biological basis
The size of its genome only
Different species evolve different life-history strategies depending on the habitat and the abiotic conditions they face.
In the equation Nt = N0 e^(rt), what does N0 represent?
The intrinsic rate of natural increase
In Nt = N0 e^(rt), N0 is the population density at time 0, the starting point of observation.
Normally, which two of the four factors (B, D, I, E) are considered the most important in determining population density?
Normally, natality and mortality are the most important of the four factors; immigration and emigration matter mainly under special conditions.
A population of bacteria growing exponentially with unlimited nutrients would, in theory:
Cover the whole earth in a short time
Any species growing exponentially would, in theory, cover the whole earth in a short time -- which never actually happens in nature because resources are always…
A population of 800 individuals has, in one year, 60 births, 90 deaths, 40 immigrants and 10 emigrants. Its density at year end is:
Interactions between two different species of organisms, which may be beneficial or harmful to one or both partners, are called:
Interspecific interactions are interactions between two different species of organisms, and may be beneficial or harmful to one or both partners.
For plants, the organisms that act as predators are:
For plants, herbivores are the predators -- grazing and browsing animals are the predators of plants.
Predators keep prey populations under control mainly so that:
No single prey species overruns the habitat
Predators keep prey populations under control, so that no single prey species overruns the habitat, thereby maintaining ecosystem balance.
Cryptic colouration, by which many prey animals blend with their surroundings, is best classified as:
Camouflage is when animals blend with their surroundings (cryptic colouration) so that predators do not detect them easily.
A natural habitat has many organisms living together that communicate and interact, for example:
Plants depending on insects for pollination
Rocks depending on soil for stability
Rivers depending on mountains for shape
Clouds depending on wind for colour
A natural habitat consists of many organisms living together, communicating and interacting -- for example, plants depend on insects for pollination.
In parasitism, the host is affected chiefly due to:
Loss of nutrients to the parasite
In parasitism, the parasite is benefited because it gets free accommodation and food, while the host is affected due to loss of nutrients.
Loss of the digestive system in many parasites is an adaptation that allows them to:
Absorb pre-digested food from the host
Digest food faster than other organisms
Live without any food at all
Loss of the digestive system allows parasites to absorb pre-digested food directly from the host, since the host has already broken it down.
Parasites typically show a high reproductive capacity chiefly to:
Offset the difficulty of reaching a new host
Reduce their dependence on the host
High reproductive capacity in parasites offsets the difficulty of reaching a new host, since many offspring fail to find a suitable host.
Lice on humans and ticks on dogs are examples of:
Ectoparasites live outside the body of the host. Examples: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, and ectoparasitic copepods on marine fish.
Plasmodium, liver fluke, tapeworm and roundworm are all examples of:
Endoparasites live inside the body of the host; examples include Plasmodium, liver fluke, tapeworm and roundworm.
Brood parasitism (nest or social parasitism) in birds is best illustrated by:
The Koel laying its eggs in the nest of a crow
A sparrow building its own nest
A parrot nesting in a tree hollow
Brood parasitism is seen in birds where the parasitic bird lays eggs in the nest of a host bird; the classic example is the Koel laying eggs in a crow's nest.
An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango tree benefits from:
Nutrients stolen from the mango's roots
Water stolen from the mango's xylem
The orchid grows as an epiphyte on the mango tree and benefits from support and better light, while the mango tree derives no apparent benefit and suffers no harm.
Barnacles growing on the back of a whale benefit chiefly by being:
Given a share of the whale's food
Barnacles growing on the back of a whale are carried to new feeding grounds; the whale is unaffected by their presence.
In the mycorrhizal association, the plant provides the fungi with:
In mycorrhizae, the fungi help the plant absorb nutrients from the soil, while the plant provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates.
In the fig-wasp mutualism, the female wasp uses the fig fruit chiefly as a site for:
The female wasp uses the fig fruit as an oviposition (egg-laying) site and uses the developing seeds within it to nourish her larvae, pollinating the fig in the process.
The Ophrys-bee relationship is considered a classic example of:
The Ophrys-bee relationship is a plant-pollinator mutualism and a classic example of co-evolution, where both species have evolved together.
Amensalism is described in this chapter as the mirror image of:
Amensalism is the mirror image of commensalism: in commensalism one gains and the other is neutral; in amensalism one loses and the other is neutral.
A population's sex ratio, age distribution and density together are called its:
Sex ratio, age distribution, density, natality and mortality are together called the attributes of a population.
A camouflaged insect that resembles a dry leaf is best understood as a defence against:
Camouflage such as resembling a dry leaf helps prey animals avoid detection by predators, and is thus a defence against predation.
A weed that releases a chemical into the soil, inhibiting the growth of nearby crop plants without itself being affected, illustrates:
This scenario, where one species (the crop) is harmed and the other (the weed) is unaffected, illustrates amensalism, a (-,0) interaction.
A cheetah chasing and killing a gazelle for food is a direct example of:
A cheetah killing and consuming a gazelle is a direct example of predation, a (+,-) interaction where the predator benefits and the prey is harmed.
Two species of birds feeding on insects at different heights of the same tree, thereby reducing competition, illustrate:
Feeding at different heights (different feeding places) on the same tree is an example of resource partitioning, which reduces the overlap between closely related…
Ectoparasitic copepods that infest many marine fish are an example of parasites that:
Live outside the body of the host
Live only inside the host's blood
Have lost the ability to reproduce
Ectoparasitic copepods live outside the body of the host fish, making them ectoparasites, similar to lice on humans and ticks on dogs.
A logistic-growth population currently at N = K/2 is growing:
In the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, the growth rate is maximum when N = K/2, since this is where the product N(K-N) is largest.
Thick layer of fat called blubber below the skin of seals in polar seas functions to:
Act as an insulator and minimise heat loss
Increase the surface area for heat radiation
Store salts absorbed from sea water
Provide buoyancy for deep diving only
In the polar seas aquatic mammals like seals have a thick layer of fat (blubber) below their skin that acts as an insulator to minimise heat loss, complementing…
A bell shaped age pyramid indicates that the population is:
The shape of the age pyramid reveals growth status: triangular means an expanding population, bell shaped means a stable population and urn shaped means a declining…
The integral form of the exponential growth equation is:
Nt = N0ert is the integral form of dN/dt = rN, where N0 is the density at time 0, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and e = 2.71828. The first option is the…
In a logistic growth curve, the final phase in which the population levels off at the carrying capacity is called the:
Logistic growth passes through a lag phase, then acceleration and deceleration phases, and finally reaches the asymptote when the population attains the carrying…
According to the Competitive Exclusion Principle, the competitively inferior species will:
Evolve immediately into a new species
Become a predator of the superior species
Always co-exist by raising its birth rate
Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resource cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively…
An orchid growing as an epiphyte on the branch of a mango tree is an example of:
The orchid gains support and better exposure to light, while the mango tree derives no apparent benefit and suffers no harm. This is a + / 0 interaction, that is…
Large climatic zones on land, produced by seasonal and regional differences in climate, are called:
Seasonal and regional differences in climate produce large climatic zones on land called biomes, e.g. desert, grassland, tropical forest, temperate forest, coniferous…
A region with very cold climate throughout the year, regardless of rainfall, is expected to support which biome?
Very cold regions give rise to the tundra biome, irrespective of precipitation.
Together, the abiotic and biotic factors of a region decide:
The rate of mutation in the organism
Together, abiotic and biotic factors decide which organism can live where, i.e. they define the organism's habitat.
A fish that can survive only within a narrow temperature range of 24–26°C is best described as:
Organisms restricted to a narrow range of temperature are called stenothermal (steno = narrow, thermal = temperature).
An organism capable of tolerating a very wide range of environmental temperatures is called:
Organisms that can tolerate a wide range of temperature are called eurythermal (eury = wide, thermal = temperature).
On land, the limiting factor for organisms is usually the ______ of water, while in the oceans it is usually the ______ of water.
On land the quantity of water (rainfall) is usually the limiting factor; in the oceans, where quantity is not a limitation, the quality of water (chiefly its salt…
The salt concentration of water, known as salinity, is expressed in units of:
The salt concentration of water is measured as salinity, expressed in parts per thousand (ppt).
An estuarine fish that can tolerate a wide range of salinities, from nearly fresh water to seawater, is described as:
Organisms that are tolerant of a wide range of salinity, such as many estuarine fishes, are called euryhaline.
In aquatic habitats, the factor corresponding to soil on land, which decides the type of bottom-dwelling (benthic) life, is:
The sediment characteristic of the bed
The surface temperature of the water
In aquatic habitats the corresponding factor to soil is the sediment characteristic of the bed, which decides the type of benthic (bottom-dwelling) life.
Certain plants of the forest floor, constantly overshadowed by tall trees, become adapted to:
Photosynthesise under very low light intensity
Absorb salts instead of light energy
Certain plants of the forest floor are constantly overshadowed by tall trees and therefore become adapted to photosynthesise under very low light intensity.
The dependence of flowering in many plants on the duration of light they receive is called:
Many plants depend on the duration of light for their flowering; this response is called photoperiodism.
The maintenance of a constant internal environment by an organism, despite a changing external environment, is called:
All organisms, in order to sustain maximum functionality, try to maintain a constant internal environment; this maintenance is called homeostasis.
When conditions become stressful, an organism may adopt one of how many broad strategies?
When conditions become stressful, an organism may adopt one of four strategies: Regulate, Conform, Migrate or Suspend.
Animals that maintain a constant body temperature and constant osmolality irrespective of outside conditions are called:
Regulators are animals with the ability to maintain a constant body temperature and a constant osmolality irrespective of the outside conditions.
All birds and mammals are examples of:
All birds and mammals are regulators, able to maintain a constant body temperature (about 37°C in mammals) irrespective of outside temperature.
Sweating in summer and shivering in winter are examples of physiological responses seen in:
Regulators, to keep body temperature constant
In summer humans sweat (evaporation cools the body) and in winter they shiver (rapid muscle contraction produces heat) — both are regulatory responses that keep body…
Organisms whose body temperature and osmotic concentration change in accordance with the surrounding medium are called:
Conformers are organisms whose body temperature changes in accordance with outside temperature; their osmotic concentration also changes with that of the surrounding…
On a graph of internal level versus external level, a regulator is represented by:
On a graph of internal level versus external level, conformers give a rising straight line, while regulators give a flat horizontal line.
Organisms that regulate their internal environment only over a limited range of external conditions, and conform beyond that range, are called:
Partial regulators regulate their internal environment over a limited range of external conditions, and beyond that range they simply conform.
A bird moving away temporarily from a stressful habitat to a more hospitable region, and returning once the stress period is over, illustrates:
Migration is escape in space: the organism moves temporarily away from the stressful habitat and returns once the stressful period is over.
An organism that ceases to be metabolically active during a stressful period and enters a period of dormancy is showing:
Escape in time, i.e. suspension of activity
Some organisms suspend all activity and enter dormancy during a stressful period; this is escape in time.
Bacteria and lower plants tide over unfavourable conditions mainly by forming:
Spores are formed in bacteria and lower plants to tide over unfavourable conditions.
Zooplankton entering a stage of suspended development during unfavourable conditions is called:
Diapause is the stage of suspended development that zooplankton enter during unfavourable conditions.
Adaptations that describe what an animal actually does, such as basking in the sun or burrowing, are classified as:
Adaptations may be physiological (internal functioning), behavioural (what the animal does) or morphological (body form and structure); basking and burrowing are…
In desert plants, a thick cuticle on the leaf surface and sunken stomata mainly serve to:
Check transpiration and reduce water loss
A thick cuticle checks transpiration, and stomata arranged in deep pits (sunken stomata) reduce water loss.
The special photosynthetic pathway in many desert plants that allows stomata to remain closed during the day, with CO2 fixed at night, is:
Desert plants possess CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism), which enables their stomata to remain closed during the day; carbon dioxide is fixed at night instead.
In Opuntia (a desert cactus), leaves are reduced to spines and photosynthesis is instead carried out by:
In desert plants like Opuntia, leaves are reduced to spines and photosynthesis is carried out by the flattened green stems.
Animals of colder regions having shorter limbs and shorter ears, which minimises heat loss, is an example of:
Shorter limbs and ears in animals of colder regions minimise heat loss; this is Allen's rule, since a smaller surface area relative to volume means less heat is…
The symptoms of altitude sickness in a newcomer to a high-altitude region typically include:
A newcomer to high altitude suffers from altitude sickness, with symptoms of nausea, fatigue and heart palpitation.
The kangaroo rat of North American deserts meets its entire water requirement through:
Drinking large amounts of standing water
Absorbing water vapour through its skin
Migrating to wetter habitats every night
The kangaroo rat meets its entire water requirement through internal oxidation of fat (metabolic water) and has the ability to concentrate its urine, so very little…
An age pyramid that is triangular in shape, with a very broad pre-reproductive base, indicates a population that is:
An expanding population gives a triangular shaped age pyramid, with a very broad pre-reproductive base.
An urn-shaped age pyramid, in which the pre-reproductive base is narrower than the reproductive middle, indicates a population that is:
A declining population gives an urn shaped age pyramid, in which the pre-reproductive base is narrower than the reproductive middle.
Population size, more technically, is referred to as:
Population size, more technically, is referred to as population density (N), which indicates the number of individuals inhabiting a particular niche.
The population density of a huge banyan tree is best expressed, according to this chapter, in terms of:
Population density need not always be counted as numbers; for a huge banyan tree it may be expressed as biomass.
The population density of grass or lichens covering an area is most appropriately expressed as:
Population density, depending on the species, may be expressed as per cent cover, as for grass or lichens.
Counting pug marks or faecal pellets is a method used to estimate the relative density of which animal, as mentioned in this chapter?
Relative density is measured for tigers, for example, by counting pug marks or faecal pellets, since measuring their absolute density directly is impractical.
Match the age pyramid shape with the correct population status: (1) Triangular with broad base (2) Bell shaped (3) Urn shaped.
A triangular pyramid with a broad base indicates an expanding population, a bell shaped pyramid a stable population, and an urn shaped pyramid a declining population.
According to the chapter, which two of the four factors changing population density are normally the most important?
Normally, natality and mortality are the most important of the four factors; immigration and emigration matter mainly under special conditions.
In a population, if (B + I) is greater than (D + E) over a given period, the population:
If (B + I) > (D + E), the population grows; if (B + I) < (D + E), it declines; if they are equal, the population is stable.
In the exponential growth equation dN/dt = (b – d) × N, the term (b – d) is replaced by which symbol to give dN/dt = rN?
r, the intrinsic rate of natural increase
Substituting (b – d) = r, where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, gives the standard exponential growth form dN/dt = rN.
In the equation N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), the symbol 'e' represents:
The intrinsic rate of natural increase
The carrying capacity of the habitat
In N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), e is the base of natural logarithms (2.71828).
A population growing exponentially, when N is plotted against time, gives a curve best described as:
Plotted against time, exponential growth gives an unbounded J-shaped curve.
The four phases through which logistic population growth passes, in correct sequence, are:
Logistic growth passes through an initial lag phase, a phase of acceleration, a phase of deceleration, and finally an asymptote at the carrying capacity.
When N is plotted against t for logistic growth, the resulting S-shaped curve is also known as the:
When N is plotted against t in logistic growth, the result is an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve, called the Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth curve.
In the logistic growth equation dN/dt = rN(K – N)/K, when N is very small compared to K, the term (K – N)/K is close to:
When N is small, (K – N)/K is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential.
In the logistic growth equation, as N approaches the carrying capacity K, the term (K – N)/K approaches:
When N approaches K, (K – N)/K approaches 0 and growth stops, i.e. dN/dt = 0.
A high intrinsic rate of natural increase (r value), which populations tend to evolve towards to survive better, is referred to in the chapter as:
Populations tend to increase their reproductive fitness so as to survive better; this is called Darwinian fitness, reflected in a high r value.
Oysters and pelagic fishes are cited in this chapter as examples of species that produce:
A small number of large-sized offspring
A large number of small-sized offspring
No offspring at all, reproducing asexually
Offspring only once in a lifetime, like salmon
Oysters and pelagic fishes are examples of species that produce a large number of small-sized offspring.
Bamboo, which flowers and dies after producing seed only once in its lifetime, is an example of a species that:
Breeds many times in a lifetime
Breeds only once in a lifetime
Is a regulator rather than a conformer
Bamboo, like the Pacific salmon fish, is cited as an example of a species that breeds only once in a lifetime.
Interactions between two different species of organisms in a habitat are called:
Interspecific interactions are interactions between two different species of organisms; they may be beneficial or harmful to one or both partners.
Interspecific interactions are classified according to their outcome for the two partners using which notation?
Interactions are classified by their outcome for the two partners as + (benefited), – (harmed) or 0 (unaffected).
For plants, the organisms that act as predators are considered to be:
Herbivores, i.e. grazing and browsing animals
For plants, herbivores are the predators; grazing and browsing animals are the predators of plants.
Since plants cannot run away from herbivores, they defend themselves mainly through:
Because plants cannot run away, they defend themselves morphologically (e.g. thorns) and chemically (e.g. secondary metabolites and poisonous chemicals).
Many animals blend with their surroundings to avoid detection by predators; this is called:
Camouflage — cryptic colouration — allows many animals to blend with their surroundings so that predators do not detect them easily.
In competition between two species, the fitness of one species is significantly lower in the presence of the other, ultimately leading to:
Immediate co-evolution into a single species
In competition, the fitness of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another species, and survival of the fittest ultimately takes place.
Parasites that live outside the body of their host are called:
Ectoparasites live outside the body of the host; examples include lice on humans and ticks on dogs.
Parasites that live inside the body of their host, such as Plasmodium and tapeworm, are called:
Endoparasites live inside the body of the host; examples include Plasmodium, liver fluke, tapeworm and roundworm.
In mutualism, also called symbiosis, the outcome for both partners is:
In mutualism or symbiosis, both the partners are benefited, written as + / +.
The Ophrys orchid and bee relationship is cited in this chapter as a classic example of:
The Ophrys orchid and bee relationship, involving sexual deceit for pollination, is a classic example of co-evolution.
Ectoparasitic copepods that infest many marine fish are an example of:
Ectoparasitic copepods that infest many marine fish are listed as ectoparasites, living outside the body of the host.
